clinicalPearls: A mitochondrial DNA depletion syndrome caused by autosomal recessive POLG variants, sitting at the severe, early-onset end of the POLG-related disorder spectrum.
Classic clinical triad of refractory seizures, psychomotor regression and hepatopathy that may progress to liver failure.
Seizures are characteristically focal, frequently occipital, with a tendency to epilepsia partialis continua and status epilepticus.
Sodium valproate is contraindicated: it can precipitate acute, often fatal, liver failure in POLG disease, and a valproate-triggered hepatic crisis is sometimes the first clue.
EEG may show rhythmic high-amplitude delta activity with superimposed (poly)spikes, a suggestive pattern.
Neuroimaging and neuropathology show cortical grey-matter degeneration (poliodystrophy) with a predilection for the occipital/calcarine cortex and relative white-matter sparing.
Liver involvement may be subclinical initially and can be unmasked or accelerated by valproate; biopsy shows microvesicular steatosis, bridging fibrosis or cirrhosis and bile-duct proliferation.
Diagnosis rests on POLG molecular testing, supported by tissue mitochondrial DNA depletion; raised blood and CSF lactate are common but not universal.
reference.pathophysiology: Alpers-Huttenlocher syndrome results from biallelic pathogenic variants in POLG, the nuclear gene encoding the catalytic subunit of mitochondrial DNA polymerase gamma, which replicates and repairs mitochondrial DNA. Impaired mitochondrial DNA replication leads to progressive quantitative depletion of mitochondrial DNA and secondary respiratory-chain deficiency, hitting post-mitotic, high-energy-demand tissues hardest, principally cortical neurons and hepatocytes. Neuronal loss, spongiform change and astrocytosis (poliodystrophy) with a striking occipital/calcarine predilection underlie the intractable focal seizures and developmental regression, while hepatocellular mitochondrial failure drives the progressive liver disease. Sodium valproate further inhibits mitochondrial function and fatty-acid oxidation, overwhelming an already compromised system and precipitating fulminant hepatic failure, which is why it is avoided. Tissue-specific thresholds for mitochondrial DNA depletion account for the characteristic combination of brain and liver disease and for the variable timing of hepatic involvement.
additionalDifferentials: Other mitochondrial DNA depletion syndromes, including hepatocerebral forms due to MPV17 or DGUOK
Other POLG-related phenotypes such as MEMSA and the ataxia-neuropathy (MIRAS/SANDO) spectrum
Progressive myoclonic epilepsies (neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis, Lafora disease, Unverricht-Lundborg disease)
Other causes of paediatric acute liver failure with encephalopathy (Wilson disease, tyrosinaemia type 1, viral hepatitis)
Non-ketotic hyperglycinaemia and other epileptic encephalopathies
Autoimmune or infective encephalitis presenting with refractory seizures
additionalInvestigations: Blood and CSF lactate (often raised) and CSF protein
Liver function tests and coagulation profile to detect hepatic synthetic failure
MRI brain (evolving occipital/cortical and thalamic or basal ganglia signal change)
EEG (focal occipital discharges, rhythmic high-amplitude delta with spikes, epilepsia partialis continua)
Liver biopsy with mitochondrial DNA quantification (microvesicular steatosis, fibrosis/cirrhosis, bile-duct proliferation)
Muscle biopsy and respiratory-chain enzyme analysis where indicated
redFlags: Valproate exposure, or planned valproate, in a child with unexplained epilepsy or regression, given the risk of fatal hepatotoxicity
Refractory focal status epilepticus or epilepsia partialis continua
Developmental regression triggered by intercurrent illness
New jaundice, coagulopathy or rising lactate signalling evolving liver failure
reference.prognosis: The disorder is progressive and usually fatal in childhood or adolescence, most often from intractable seizures or liver failure. Liver transplantation is generally not advised because of the underlying multisystem mitochondrial disease and poor neurological outcome.
pitfalls: Prescribing sodium valproate for seizures before considering POLG disease, which can precipitate fatal liver failure.
Assuming normal early liver function and lactate exclude the diagnosis; hepatic disease may appear later.
Delaying diagnosis because early MRI and lactate can be normal; POLG testing should be pursued on clinical suspicion.
Attributing the hepatopathy to an unrelated cause when it is part of the syndrome.
Considering liver transplantation without recognising the systemic mitochondrial nature of the disease.
management: Avoid sodium valproate absolutely, as it can precipitate fatal hepatic failure in POLG disease
Control seizures with alternative antiseizure medications, managing status epilepticus and epilepsia partialis continua under neurology guidance
Provide supportive care with nutritional support and gastrostomy feeding, physiotherapy and management of developmental regression
Monitor hepatic function and coagulation for progressive liver disease and synthetic failure
Recognise that liver transplantation is generally not advised because of the multisystem mitochondrial disease and poor neurological outcome
Coordinate multidisciplinary metabolic, neurology and palliative care given the progressive, life-limiting course
Offer genetic counselling and family testing for this autosomal recessive disorder
